classification.classification_note: The manifested crash is an ASan stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 3. The underlying bug is an out-of-bounds read from a zero-length `HasRouteTlv` body.

bug_description.normalized: In the staged vulnerable `71d40a5c838d345248fbc130c74182dda99d85f1` tree, the exact 82-byte `ip6-send-fuzzer` witness (SHA256 `bed0dada222336406e91759d9f431b943becc71a0026aa3eef3ae43a9de86f28`) makes the harness set `isSecure = true` and send the remaining bytes through OpenThread's local IPv6/UDP/CoAP path until CoAP dispatches the Server Data resource to `Leader::HandleServerData()`. That handler copies the attacker-controlled Thread Network Data TLV into stack `ThreadNetworkDataTlv networkData` and forwards `networkData.GetTlvs()` / `networkData.GetLength()` into `RegisterNetworkData()`. The saved ASan stack fixes the later control path to `RegisterNetworkData` line 587, so the crash comes from the `!rlocIn` arm calling `AddNetworkData(aTlvs, aTlvsLength)`. `AddNetworkData()` interprets a top-level Prefix TLV from that buffer, `AddPrefix()` interprets a nested Has Route sub-TLV, and `AddHasRoute()` tries to append one `HasRouteEntry` to leader state. The reproduced AddressSanitizer report says the 3-byte source read begins exactly at offset 289, one byte past stack `networkData` `[32,289)`, while `AddHasRoute()` reads from `aHasRoute.GetEntry(0)` and `HasRouteTlv` contains only the 2-byte base TLV header before its entries. That means the dispatched Has Route TLV header occupies the final two bytes of `networkData` and has zero entry bytes. Vulnerable `AddHasRoute()` nevertheless executes `memcpy(..., aHasRoute.GetEntry(0), sizeof(HasRouteEntry))` without first checking `aHasRoute.GetNumEntries() > 0`, so it reads three bytes from the first byte past `networkData`, matching the saved `AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 3` at `network_data_leader_ftd.cpp:690`. The fix adds that missing `GetNumEntries() > 0` guard and propagates the resulting parse error back through `AddPrefix()` and `AddNetworkData()`.

source.description: First bug-relevant project statement on the reproduced path that materializes attacker-controlled Thread Network Data bytes into stack object `networkData`.
source.value_from: The staged 82-byte witness file `poc` contains ASCII `a/sd`, and the saved crash stack shows `ot::Coap::Coap::ProcessReceivedRequest` dispatching into `HandleServerData()`. This statement is where the current request's Thread Network Data TLV becomes a project-visible stack buffer.

tainted_value_origin.description: This call forwards the current stack-resident Network Data byte span into `RegisterNetworkData()`. The same bytes are later reparsed as a `PrefixTlv`, then as a zero-length `HasRouteTlv`, and finally read through `aHasRoute.GetEntry(0)` at the crash site.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer crash site. `AddHasRoute()` copies one 3-byte `HasRouteEntry` from the attacker-controlled `aHasRoute` object even though that TLV has zero entry bytes, so the source pointer is already one-past-end of stack `networkData`.
sink.note: The saved ASan trace reports `AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 3` here and identifies local stack `networkData` in `HandleServerData()` as the over-read object `[32,289)` with the access beginning at offset 289.

root_cause.description: Missing precondition check: the copy site assumes the dispatched `HasRouteTlv` contains at least one full 3-byte `HasRouteEntry`, but vulnerable code never enforces `aHasRoute.GetNumEntries() > 0` before reading entry 0.
root_cause.note: The fixing diff adds `VerifyOrExit(aHasRoute.GetNumEntries() > 0, error = OT_ERROR_PARSE);` before this `memcpy`, then propagates that parse failure through `SuccessOrExit(error = AddHasRoute(...))` in `AddPrefix()` and `SuccessOrExit(error = AddPrefix(...))` in `AddNetworkData()`.

parser_admitted.description: By this point CoAP request parsing has already matched the Server Data resource and dispatches into `Leader::HandleServerData()`, so nested Thread TLV registration parsing proceeds on attacker-controlled bytes.

coarse_trace.summary: The received packet is admitted as a CoAP request on the Server Data resource and dispatched to `Leader::HandleServerData()`.
The leader-side handler copies the request's `ThreadNetworkDataTlv` into stack `networkData` and forwards its raw TLV span into `RegisterNetworkData()`.

The saved stack fixes execution to `RegisterNetworkData` line 587, so the `!rlocIn` arm reparses the current TLV span through `AddNetworkData()`, which selects a top-level Prefix TLV and then a nested Has Route sub-TLV.

The selected `HasRouteTlv` contributes only its final 2-byte TLV header and no entry bytes, but `AddHasRoute()` still copies one 3-byte `HasRouteEntry` from `aHasRoute.GetEntry(0)`, over-reading past stack `networkData`.

fine_trace.note: Source. After CoAP dispatch admits the Server Data request, this statement copies the current request's Thread Network Data TLV into stack `networkData`, materializing the bytes later reinterpreted as `PrefixTlv` and `HasRouteTlv` objects.
The handler forwards the extracted TLV span and the sender-derived RLOC16 into leader registration. Every later source-side read at the sink comes from this same stack-resident `networkData` buffer.
The saved ASan stack pins `RegisterNetworkData` at line 587, which is the `!rlocIn` arm. This call hands the current TLV span directly to `AddNetworkData()` for parsing and merging.
While iterating the current `aTlvs` span, the selected top-level Network Data TLV has type Prefix, so its bytes are reinterpreted as `PrefixTlv aPrefix` and handed to `AddPrefix()`.
Within that prefix, a nested sub-TLV has type Has Route, so `AddPrefix()` reinterprets the current bytes as `HasRouteTlv` and dispatches `AddHasRoute()` on them.

fine_trace.code: uint8_t GetNumEntries(void) const { return GetLength() / sizeof(HasRouteEntry); }
fine_trace.note: For the dispatched `aHasRoute`, the TLV contributes zero bytes of entry payload after its 2-byte TLV header. That is the only layout consistent with the saved ASan report: the later 3-byte source read starts exactly at `networkData` offset 289, one byte past the 257-byte object, and `GetEntry(0)` begins immediately after the header. With `GetLength() == 0`, this method returns zero entries.

With `i == 0`, `GetEntry(0)` returns the first byte after the Has Route TLV header. Because step 6 established that this TLV has zero entry bytes, that pointer is the first byte past stack `networkData`.

Sink and root cause. The function nevertheless copies `sizeof(HasRouteEntry) == 3` bytes from `aHasRoute.GetEntry(0)` into leader state. Because step 7's source pointer already points one-past-end of stack `networkData`, this `memcpy` performs the saved 3-byte out-of-bounds read. No preceding `aHasRoute.GetNumEntries() > 0` guard blocks the copy.

allocation_context.note: ASan reports the over-read object as local stack `networkData`, occupying `[32,289)` in this frame.

crash_stack.function: ot::Ip6::Ip6::HandleDatagram(ot::Message&, ot::Ip6::Netif*, signed char, void const*, bool)

sanitizer_ground_truth.source: parsed from staged sanitizer_trace.txt, default_crash_trace.txt, reproduction_report.json, vulnerable source, and patch.diff

cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: The saved ASan stack directly covers fine-trace steps 3-8 (`RegisterNetworkData -> AddNetworkData -> AddPrefix -> AddHasRoute -> __asan_memcpy`). Earlier materialization steps 1-2 are reconstructed from the only `HandleServerData()` call site that copies `networkData` and forwards it into `RegisterNetworkData()`.
cross_validation.tainted_value_reaches_sink: Yes. Step 1 materializes current request bytes into stack `networkData`, step 2 forwards that span as `aTlvs`, steps 4-5 reinterpret those same bytes as `PrefixTlv` and `HasRouteTlv`, step 7 computes one-past-end `aHasRoute.GetEntry(0)` from that same object, and step 8 reads from it.
cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The fixing diff adds `VerifyOrExit(aHasRoute.GetNumEntries() > 0, error = OT_ERROR_PARSE);` at the start of `AddHasRoute()`, then propagates that parse failure through `SuccessOrExit(error = AddHasRoute(...))` in `AddPrefix()` and `SuccessOrExit(error = AddPrefix(...))` in `AddNetworkData()`. For the witnessed zero-length `HasRouteTlv`, the new guard stops before `memcpy` can read past `networkData`.

poc.trigger: The staged 82-byte witness file `poc` reproduced the saved AddressSanitizer crash under `ip6-send-fuzzer` via `PYTHONPATH=gt_generation python3 -m gt_toolkit arvo-workspace --result-dir /mnt/datastore/gt_generation/gt_results/arvo_3280 run --version vulnerable --expect crash`, yielding crash stack `ot::NetworkData::Leader::AddHasRoute -> AddPrefix -> AddNetworkData`.

format.name: OpenThread ip6-send CoAP Server Data request
format.contract: The trigger contract is the exact staged 82-byte `ip6-send-fuzzer` input saved as `poc` (SHA256 `bed0dada222336406e91759d9f431b943becc71a0026aa3eef3ae43a9de86f28`). Its first byte sets `isSecure = true`; the remaining bytes are admitted through OpenThread's IPv6/UDP/CoAP receive path and dispatch the Server Data handler. On the witnessed path, the extracted Thread Network Data TLV contains a Prefix TLV whose trailing `HasRouteTlv` occupies the final two bytes of stack `networkData` and has zero entry bytes, so `AddHasRoute()` later executes `memcpy(..., aHasRoute.GetEntry(0), sizeof(HasRouteEntry))` with the source pointer already one-past-end.
